lessons.title: Case Study: How Risk Parity Behaved in 2008, 2020, and 2022

children.text: The last lesson spent an entire discussion warning against confident-sounding backtest numbers that skip walk-forward re-estimation, financing costs, and execution lags. It would be a strange way to follow that up by handing you a precise, fabricated return figure for exactly what this course's Nifty, G-Sec, and gold portfolio would have earned in 2008, 2020, or 2022, without the real NAV histories and rolling methodology the last lesson insisted on. Instead, this lesson does something more honest: it walks through what is well documented about each episode, index levels, RBI policy actions, and the rupee, and reasons through the mechanism, the direction each sleeve should have moved and why, while being explicit about where a genuine number requires the methodology from the last lesson applied to real data.

Nifty 50 fell from a January 2008 high above 6,300 to a low around 2,500 by late October and November 2008, a peak-to-trough decline of more than half, among the sharpest drawdowns in the index's history. The RBI's response, once the Lehman Brothers collapse in September 2008 turned a slowdown into a full liquidity crisis, was a rapid series of rate cuts, taking the repo rate from around 9% down to roughly 4.75% by early 2009. That combination, flight to safety plus aggressive monetary easing, is exactly the mechanism behind the negative equity-debt correlation this course has assumed throughout: falling growth expectations push both equity down and rates down, and falling rates push bond prices up.

Gold's path was more complicated. In the most acute weeks of the crisis, gold saw a liquidity-driven selloff alongside equity, the same margin-call mechanism covered in chapter 3's discussion of crisis correlation, as leveraged holders sold whatever they could to raise cash. It then recovered and rallied meaningfully through 2009 as a safe haven. INR-denominated gold returns were further boosted by the rupee's own sharp depreciation against the dollar over the same stretch, from around 39-40 to nearly 50, since gold is priced in dollars internationally and a weaker rupee mechanically raises the domestic price.

body.text: Mechanically, 2008 looks like the textbook regime this course's case studies have assumed by default: debt, and gold after its brief initial wobble, both moved to offset a severe equity drawdown. A portfolio weighted the way this course's ERC solutions have been, roughly 20% equity and closer to 80% between debt and gold, would mechanically have absorbed only a fraction of Nifty's decline, for the reasons chapters 2 and 3 laid out.

children.text: Chapter 3 already covered the core facts: Nifty 50 fell from just above 12,400 in mid-January 2020 to an intraday low near 7,511 on 23 March 2020, close to a 40% decline in about ten weeks, sharp enough to trip SEBI's market-wide circuit breaker that morning. Gold sold off alongside equity in the most acute days of the panic, the same liquidity-driven mechanism as 2008, before decoupling and rallying to fresh highs later in 2020 as the initial scramble for cash eased. The RBI cut the repo rate from 5.15% to 4.40% at an emergency meeting on 27 March 2020, then further to 4.00% by May 2020, supportive for bond prices through most of the year, though the most acute days of March saw stress and reduced liquidity across nearly every market, government bonds included.

body.text: March 2020 is the cleanest real-world illustration of chapter 3's 'correlations go to 1 in a crash' lesson. Even a well-constructed risk parity portfolio's usual diversifiers wobbled in the most acute days, gold included, only recovering their offsetting behaviour once the immediate liquidity panic passed. A risk parity portfolio is built to behave better than a pure equity book through a typical drawdown, not to be immune to the first, sharpest days of a genuine liquidity crisis.

children.text: Also already covered in chapter 3: the RBI raised the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50% between May 2022 and February 2023 to fight inflation, Nifty 50 corrected from its October 2021 peak into a 2022 low around June, and 10-year G-Sec yields rose as prices fell, moving with equity rather than against it. Gold had a genuinely difficult year for much of 2022 in dollar terms, as aggressive US Federal Reserve hiking strengthened the dollar, a typical headwind for gold. But INR-denominated gold returns were cushioned, and at times boosted, by the rupee's own depreciation against the dollar over 2022, from around 74-75 to briefly beyond 83, a reminder that an Indian gold ETF holder's returns are not the same as a global dollar-based gold investor's returns. Currency effects are a real, separate return driver on top of gold's own dollar price.

body.text: 2022 is the one episode among these three where the portfolio's usual diversification mechanism did not just wobble briefly, it broke down structurally for months, exactly as chapter 3's correlation regime lesson described. Debt failed to offset equity because both were responding to the same inflation and rate shock. If gold provided any real cushioning that year, currency depreciation was likely a meaningful part of why, not gold's dollar price alone.

children.text: What This Actually Tells You, and What It Doesn't

Everything above describes direction and mechanism using well-documented facts: index levels, RBI policy decisions, and the rupee's path. None of it is a verified, walk-forward-backtested return series for a specific G-Sec fund or gold ETF through any of these three windows, and this lesson has deliberately avoided inventing one. Producing an honest, precise answer to 'what would this exact portfolio have returned in 2008' requires exactly the methodology from the last lesson: real NAV histories for your chosen instruments, rolling weight re-estimation, a realistic execution lag, and financing costs if any leverage was involved, applied by you to real data, not asserted in a lesson.

body.text: This lesson's historical figures (index levels, RBI rate changes, USD/INR levels) reflect general knowledge of these well-publicized episodes and are given as approximate context, not precise, sourced data points. Before using any of them in real analysis or reporting, verify exact figures against primary sources: NSE's own historical index data and RBI's official monetary policy statements and press releases.

children.text: This is itself the final, meta point of chapter 4's backtesting discussion. Be as skeptical of a confident-sounding historical narrative as of a suspicious backtest number. If a claim about how a strategy performed in a specific year cannot be traced back to actual data and a stated methodology, treat it as illustrative at best, exactly the same discipline the last lesson asked you to apply to any levered risk parity return you encounter.

body.title: Three Stress Regimes for Risk Parity

events.title: Lehman Collapse and the GFC Trough
events.description: Nifty falls more than half from its January 2008 high; RBI begins an aggressive easing cycle that supports bonds, after an initial liquidity-driven wobble in most risk assets including gold.

events.title: COVID Liquidity Panic
events.description: Nifty falls close to 40% in ten weeks; SEBI's circuit breaker trips on 23 March; gold briefly sells off with equity before decoupling and rallying for the rest of the year.

events.title: The Inflation-Shock Regime
events.description: RBI raises the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50%; equity and debt fall together for months, the clearest real-world break in risk parity's usual diversification mechanism covered in this course.

body.title: Which Year Was Hardest for Risk Parity?
body.scenario: A colleague asks you to rank 2008, 2020, and 2022 from best to worst for a Nifty, G-Sec, and gold risk parity portfolio, using only the mechanism described in this lesson, not a precise backtest.
body.prompt: How would you rank them, and what is the reasoning?
body.modelAnswer: 2022 was almost certainly the hardest of the three for this specific portfolio, because it is the one episode where debt structurally failed to offset equity for an extended period, both fell together for months due to the shared inflation and rate shock, exactly the correlation regime breakdown chapter 3 described. 2008 and 2020 both saw brief, sharp liquidity-driven wobbles in the usual diversifiers, gold in both cases, and even bonds briefly in March 2020, but in both years the traditional offsetting relationship reasserted itself relatively quickly as central banks eased aggressively. Between 2008 and 2020, without real data it is hard to rank precisely, but the shared feature, rate cuts restoring debt's offsetting role within weeks to months, is present in both, unlike 2022's multi-quarter regime shift.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why does this lesson describe 2022 as structurally different from 2008 and 2020 for a risk parity portfolio, rather than just another difficult year?
options: Because Nifty fell by a larger percentage in 2022 than in the other two years

Because in 2008 and 2020, debt's offsetting relationship with equity reasserted itself within weeks to months as rates were cut, while in 2022 debt and equity fell together for an extended period because both were driven by the same inflation and rate-hiking shock
Because gold was not available as an investable asset in 2022
Because SEBI suspended circuit breakers during 2022
body.explanation: Nifty's 2022 correction was actually smaller than either 2008's or 2020's. What made 2022 structurally different was duration and mechanism: debt's usual negative correlation with equity depends on a growth-driven regime where weak growth brings both equity weakness and rate cuts. 2022 was an inflation-driven regime instead, where rate hikes to fight inflation hurt bond prices at the same time high rates and inflation fears hurt equity, removing the offsetting relationship for months rather than days.

body.text: 2008 and 2020 both tested risk parity's diversification mechanism briefly and it held, after an initial, well-documented wobble in gold. 2022 tested a different, more dangerous failure mode: a genuine, months-long correlation regime shift that this course's chapter 3 explained in the abstract and 2022 delivered in reality. Knowing the difference between a brief liquidity wobble and a structural regime shift, and being honest about what you can and cannot verify without real data, matters more than any single historical return figure.

points: 2008: Nifty fell more than half; RBI's aggressive post-Lehman rate cuts supported debt; gold wobbled briefly in the acute liquidity crunch before rallying, aided further by rupee depreciation.

March 2020: Nifty fell close to 40% in ten weeks with a circuit breaker trigger; gold sold off alongside equity in the most acute days, the clearest real-world case of chapter 3's crisis correlation, before decoupling and rallying.

2022: the RBI's inflation-fighting rate hikes drove equity and debt down together for months, a structural break in risk parity's usual diversification mechanism, not a brief wobble; gold's dollar weakness was partly offset by rupee depreciation.

This lesson deliberately avoided inventing precise portfolio return figures for any of these episodes. A defensible answer requires the walk-forward, financing-aware backtesting methodology from the last lesson applied to real NAV data, not a narrative.

Treat confident historical performance claims with the same skepticism chapter 4 asked you to apply to suspicious backtests: if you cannot see the data and the methodology, it is illustrative at best.
The final lesson of this course puts all of this together: building a working risk parity portfolio in Python using real NSE and BSE data, from data collection through honest evaluation.
